title: Fitting a shower valve and riser bar on a gravity system
subtitle: Install a thermostatic bar-valve shower with riser and adjustable head, connected to the gravity hot and cold supplies in the bathroom
excerpt: How to install a thermostatic shower valve and riser bar on a gravity-fed hot and cold supply. Covers planning the pipe routes, connecting supplies to the valve, fitting the riser bar and head, connecting the waste, and testing flow.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade plumbing practice for shower installation and Water Regulations Advisory Scheme guidance (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A shower mixing valve with a temperature-regulating cartridge that maintains the set water temperature even when other taps are opened elsewhere in the building. It has a maximum temperature stop factory-set to 38 or 43 degrees Celsius. Required under Part G of the Building Regulations for showers serving baths.

A domestic hot and cold water supply where the pressure comes from the height difference between the storage tanks in the loft and the outlets below, rather than from mains pressure. Flow rate depends on the head height: at least 1 metre of head above the shower head is needed for an acceptable shower flow.

A vertical chrome or stainless bar fixed to the shower wall that carries the sliding shower head bracket and the flexible hose. The shower head slides up and down the bar to adjust the height. The riser is fixed at the top and bottom to the wall with concealed or exposed fixings.

Check the head height and plan pipe routes

Measure the vertical distance from the cold-water storage tank base in the loft to the shower valve position. A minimum of 1 m of head above the valve is recommended for a gravity-fed thermostatic valve; 1.5 m or more gives a comfortable flow. If the head is less than 1 m, a shower pump is needed and the thermostatic valve may need to be changed for a type rated for pumped systems.
Connect hot and cold supplies to the valve

Turn off the water supplies. Run 15 mm hot and cold pipes to the valve position, fitting isolating valves on each supply for future maintenance. Connect the supply pipes to the valve inlets, applying PTFE tape to all male threads. The cold supply connects to the left (or the inlet marked C) and the hot to the right (marked H): reversing the connections causes the valve to over-heat.
Fix the riser bar and connect the hose

Fix the riser bar to the wall using the spirit level, drilling into tile with a diamond tile drill at low speed with water cooling. The hose connects from the valve outlet to the riser bar inlet at the bottom of the bar. Use the rubber washers supplied and do not over-tighten chrome fittings.

Connect the shower tray waste to the soil stack or nearest waste stack with a minimum 18 mm per metre gradient. Restore the water supply, open the isolating valves, and test the shower at low temperature first to check all connections are watertight. Adjust the temperature limiter on the valve body if required before closing up the wall finish.

attrs.symptom: Water runs from only hot or only cold through the valve
attrs.cause: Hot and cold supplies are connected to the wrong inlets on the valve body.
attrs.fix: Isolate the supplies, swap the supply connections at the valve, restore the water, and test.

attrs.symptom: Flow rate is poor even at maximum setting
attrs.cause: Insufficient head on a gravity system, or the isolating valve on one supply is only partially open.
attrs.fix: Confirm both isolating valves are fully open. Measure the available head. If under 1 m, fit an inline shower pump rated for the valve type.
